content: Cystic fibrosis (CF) is a severe genetic disorder that affects over 90,000 individuals globally. While it impacts multiple organs, the damage to the airways is the most significant factor influencing both quality of life and survival. In CF, early airway infections are often caused by Staphylococcus aureus, while Pseudomonas aeruginosa becomes more prevalent in later stages of the disease. Macrolide antibiotics, such as azithromycin and clarithromycin, are commonly administered orally. These antibiotics are effective against a broad range of bacteria, including gram-positive organisms like S. aureus and some gram-negative bacteria like Haemophilus influenzae. Beyond their antimicrobial properties, macrolides may also modulate airway inflammation and infection, which are hallmarks of CF. They are generally well-tolerated, cost-effective, and widely used, but their extensive use has contributed to the emergence of antibiotic-resistant bacteria. The purpose of this review was to evaluate the potential benefits and harms of macrolide antibiotics in individuals with CF. If benefits were identified, the review aimed to determine the optimal type, dosage, and duration of macrolide therapy. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving macrolide antibiotics in both children and adults with CF. Comparisons were made between macrolides and placebo, other antibiotic classes, different macrolides, or varying doses and administration methods of the same macrolide. The review included 14 studies with a total of 1,467 participants, lasting between 28 days and 36 months. All studies focused on azithromycin. Eleven studies compared oral azithromycin to placebo, one compared high-dose to low-dose azithromycin, one compared nebulized to oral azithromycin, and one compared weekly to daily dosing. Oral Azithromycin vs. Placebo At up to six months, azithromycin showed a modest improvement in lung function, as measured by forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1% predicted), compared to placebo (mean difference [MD] 3.97%, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.74 to 6.19; high-certainty evidence). However, no significant differences were observed at three months (MD 2.70%, 95% CI -0.12 to 5.52) or 12 months (MD -0.13%, 95% CI -4.96 to 4.70). Participants receiving azithromycin likely had a reduced risk of pulmonary exacerbations and a longer time to the first exacerbation (hazard ratio [HR] 0.61, 95% CI 0.50 to 0.75; moderate-certainty evidence). Mild side effects were common but did not differ significantly between the azithromycin and placebo groups (moderate-certainty evidence). There was no difference in hospital admission rates at six months (odds ratio [OR] 0.61, 95% CI 0.36 to 1.04; high-certainty evidence) or in the acquisition of P. aeruginosa at 12 months (HR 1.00, 95% CI 0.64 to 1.55; moderate-certainty evidence). High-Dose vs. Low-Dose Azithromycin The evidence was insufficient to determine whether there were differences in FEV1% predicted at six months or in the rate of exacerbations per child per month (MD -0.05, 95% CI -0.20 to 0.10; very low-certainty evidence). This study included only children and did not report on other clinically significant outcomes. Nebulized Azithromycin vs. Oral Azithromycin Data from this comparison could not be included in the analysis, and all evidence was graded as very low certainty. The study reported a greater mean improvement in FEV1% predicted at one month in the nebulized azithromycin group (P < 0.001). However, it is unclear whether there was any change in P. aeruginosa counts. Weekly vs. Daily Azithromycin Weekly dosing was associated with a smaller mean improvement in FEV1% predicted at six months compared to daily dosing (MD -0.70%, 95% CI -0.95 to -0.45; moderate-certainty evidence). Weekly dosing likely resulted in a longer time to the first exacerbation (MD 17.30 days, 95% CI 4.32 to 30.28 days; moderate-certainty evidence). Gastrointestinal side effects were more common with weekly dosing, but there was likely no difference in hospital admissions or quality of life between the two groups. Authors' Conclusions Azithromycin therapy is associated with modest but consistent improvements in respiratory function, a reduced risk of pulmonary exacerbations, and a longer time to the first exacerbation over six months. However, evidence for its efficacy beyond six months is limited. Azithromycin appears to have a favorable safety profile, though weekly dosing is associated with more gastrointestinal side effects, making it less suitable for long-term use. The treatment burden is relatively low, and the medication is inexpensive. A significant concern is the emergence of macrolide-resistant bacteria, as reported in the most recent study. Combined with the lack of long-term data, the current evidence does not strongly support azithromycin therapy for all individuals with CF. Future research should focus on longer-term outcomes using validated tools and consistent reporting to facilitate data synthesis. Studies should also report on important adverse events, such as hearing impairment and liver disease. Additional data on different methods of azithromycin administration and their effects on primary outcomes would aid in decision-making. Finally, it is crucial to evaluate azithromycin therapy in individuals with CF who are receiving newer cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) modulator therapies, as none of the trials included in this review addressed this population.
